defects-diffusion-001.question: Among point defects in ionic crystals, which correctly describes a Frenkel defect?
choices: A pair consisting of a cation vacancy and an anion vacancy, formed together so as to keep the whole crystal electrically neutral
A pair of a vacancy and an interstitial ion, formed when an ion moves from its lattice site into an interstitial position
A substitutional impurity defect, in which an ion of an element different from the host occupies a lattice site in place of a host ion
defects-diffusion-001.explanation: A Frenkel defect forms when an ion (usually the smaller cation) moves from its lattice site to an interstitial position, creating a vacancy and an interstitial ion as a pair. Ag⁺ in AgCl and AgBr is the well-known example. A pair of a cation vacancy and an anion vacancy is a Schottky defect, which occurs mainly in NaCl and MgO. Both combinations preserve the electrical neutrality of the crystal as a whole. Substitution by a foreign ion is impurity solid solution; when the valences differ, vacancies or other defects are introduced to compensate the charge.

defects-diffusion-002.question: Which correctly describes the relation between the Burgers vector and the dislocation line of an edge dislocation?
choices: They are perpendicular to each other
They are parallel to each other
They always make an angle of 45°
defects-diffusion-002.explanation: An edge dislocation has the form of an extra half-plane of atoms inserted into the crystal, and its Burgers vector b is perpendicular to the dislocation line. An edge dislocation glides in the direction of b, and its slip plane is uniquely defined as the plane containing both b and the line. b is parallel to the line in a screw dislocation; because a screw dislocation has no unique slip plane, it can cross-slip onto another slip plane. Most real dislocations are mixed dislocations in between, with the proportions of edge and screw character changing continuously along the line, so there is no fixed 45°.

defects-diffusion-003.question: A metal has a vacancy formation energy of 0.90 eV. Using n/N = exp(−Q/kT), which value is closest to the equilibrium vacancy concentration (the fraction of lattice sites that are vacant) at 1000 K? Take Boltzmann's constant as k = 8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K.
choices: About 5.4×10⁻³
About 2.9×10⁻⁵
About 3.6×10⁻¹¹
defects-diffusion-003.explanation: kT = 8.617×10⁻⁵ × 1000 ≈ 0.0862 eV, so Q/kT = 0.90/0.0862 ≈ 10.44. Then n/N = exp(−10.44) ≈ 2.9×10⁻⁵, or one vacancy for roughly every 35,000 lattice sites. About 5.4×10⁻³ is the mistake of halving the exponent to exp(−Q/2kT), confusing it with the expression for the carrier density of an intrinsic semiconductor. About 3.6×10⁻¹¹ is the mistake of computing 10 to the power −10.44 with a common logarithm instead of exp. The vacancy concentration rises exponentially with temperature and reaches around 10⁻⁴ near the melting point.

defects-diffusion-004.question: Carbon diffuses at steady state through a 5.0 mm thick steel plate whose two faces are held at carbon concentrations of 1.2 kg/m³ and 0.8 kg/m³. If the diffusion coefficient is 3.0×10⁻¹¹ m²/s, which value is closest to the diffusion flux of carbon? Assume the concentration varies linearly through the thickness.
choices: About 2.4×10⁻¹² kg/(m²·s)
About 7.2×10⁻⁹ kg/(m²·s)
About 2.4×10⁻⁹ kg/(m²·s)
defects-diffusion-004.explanation: At steady state, Fick's first law J = −D(dC/dx) applies. The concentration gradient is (0.8 − 1.2)/(5.0×10⁻³ m) = −80 kg/m⁴, so J = 3.0×10⁻¹¹ × 80 = 2.4×10⁻⁹ kg/(m²·s), flowing from the high-concentration side to the low-concentration side. About 2.4×10⁻¹² is a unit-conversion error from dividing by the thickness left as 5.0 in mm, and about 7.2×10⁻⁹ uses the concentration on one side, 1.2 kg/m³, instead of the concentration difference. It is the concentration difference that drives the flow, so getting the gradient right matters. The same approach is used in hydrogen permeation tests and in evaluating gas separation membranes.

defects-diffusion-005.question: The diffusion coefficient of carbon in γ-iron follows the Arrhenius form D = D₀exp(−Q/RT) with D₀ = 2.3×10⁻⁵ m²/s and activation energy Q = 148 kJ/mol. Which value is closest to the diffusion coefficient at 927 °C? Take the gas constant as R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
choices: About 8.3×10⁻¹² m²/s
About 1.1×10⁻¹³ m²/s
About 2.3×10⁻⁵ m²/s
defects-diffusion-005.explanation: Convert the temperature to absolute temperature: T = 927 + 273 = 1200 K. Q/RT = 148000/(8.314 × 1200) ≈ 14.83, so D = 2.3×10⁻⁵ × exp(−14.83) ≈ 2.3×10⁻⁵ × 3.6×10⁻⁷ ≈ 8.3×10⁻¹² m²/s. About 1.1×10⁻¹³ is the mistake of substituting the temperature as 927 in °C. About 2.3×10⁻⁵ is the mistake of leaving Q as 148 in kJ, which makes the exponent nearly zero and gives almost the same value as D₀. Because D changes exponentially with temperature, raising the carburizing temperature by just a few tens of degrees can shorten the treatment time considerably.

defects-diffusion-006.question: The diffusion coefficient of an element was 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ m²/s at 800 K and 4.0×10⁻¹³ m²/s at 1000 K. Assuming the Arrhenius form D = D₀exp(−Q/RT), which value is closest to the activation energy Q? Take R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
choices: About 53 kJ/mol
About 123 kJ/mol
About 245 kJ/mol
defects-diffusion-006.explanation: Taking the ratio of the expressions at the two temperatures eliminates D₀ and gives ln(D₂/D₁) = (Q/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂). D₂/D₁ = 40, ln 40 ≈ 3.689 and 1/800 − 1/1000 = 2.5×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, so Q = 8.314 × 3.689 / (2.5×10⁻⁴) ≈ 1.23×10⁵ J/mol, about 123 kJ/mol. About 53 kJ/mol uses the common logarithm (log₁₀ 40 ≈ 1.602) instead of the natural logarithm, and about 245 kJ/mol is double the value, from confusing the expression with the form exp(−Q/2RT). In practice, ln D is plotted against 1/T and Q is obtained from the slope −Q/R of the straight line.

defects-diffusion-007.question: A steel containing 0.20 wt% carbon is carburized with its surface carbon concentration held at 1.00 wt%. Which value is closest to the time needed for the carbon concentration to reach 0.60 wt% at a depth of 0.50 mm? Take the diffusion coefficient as 1.6×10⁻¹¹ m²/s, (C − C₀)/(Cₛ − C₀) = 1 − erf(x/2√(Dt)), erf(0.371) = 0.40 and erf(0.477) = 0.50.
choices: About 7.9 hours
About 19 hours
About 4.8 hours
defects-diffusion-007.explanation: (0.60 − 0.20)/(1.00 − 0.20) = 0.50, so 1 − erf(z) = 0.50 and erf(z) = 0.50 give z = x/2√(Dt) = 0.477. Then √(Dt) = 0.50×10⁻³/(2 × 0.477) ≈ 5.24×10⁻⁴ m, Dt ≈ 2.75×10⁻⁷ m², and t = 2.75×10⁻⁷/(1.6×10⁻¹¹) ≈ 1.72×10⁴ s, about 4.8 hours. About 19 hours is the mistake of dropping the 2 in the denominator and setting x/√(Dt) = 0.477, which makes the time four times too long. About 7.9 hours ignores the initial carbon concentration C₀ and uses 0.60/1.00, giving erf(z) = 0.40 and z = 0.371. Because the time is proportional to the square of the depth, how the factors are handled has a large effect.

defects-diffusion-008.question: In a diffusion treatment at a fixed temperature, by what factor must the treatment time be increased to double the depth at which a given concentration is reached?
choices: 2 times
About 1.4 times (√2 times)
4 times
defects-diffusion-008.explanation: In the error-function solution the concentration depends only on x/2√(Dt), so the depth x at which a given concentration is reached is proportional to √(Dt). At the same temperature D is constant, so doubling the depth requires doubling √t, that is, four times the time. Two times assumes the depth is proportional to time, and √2 times applies the proportionality the wrong way round. The diffusion-distance estimate x ≈ √(Dt) is used in many situations, including carburizing and dopant diffusion. When a deep layer is needed, raising the temperature to increase D is more effective than extending the time.

defects-diffusion-009.question: In α-iron at the same temperature, the diffusion coefficient of carbon is many orders of magnitude larger than that of nickel. Which is the main reason?
choices: Carbon moves between interstitial sites, so it can jump even without a neighboring vacancy
Carbon diffuses by the vacancy mechanism, and vacancies tend to gather around carbon atoms
Carbon has a smaller atomic mass than nickel, so its thermal vibrations are faster
defects-diffusion-009.explanation: Small atoms such as carbon sit in the gaps between iron atoms (interstitial sites) and can jump one after another into neighboring empty interstitial sites. Since almost all interstitial sites are empty, jump opportunities are plentiful and the activation energy is small. Substitutional atoms such as nickel diffuse by the vacancy mechanism and can move only when a vacancy arrives next to them; the vacancy formation energy is added to the activation energy, making diffusion far slower. The difference in vibration frequency due to atomic mass plays a minor role, but only the difference in diffusion mechanism can explain a gap of many orders of magnitude.

defects-diffusion-010.question: Which statement about diffusion paths in a polycrystalline metal is correct?
choices: The activation energy generally increases in the order lattice diffusion < grain boundary diffusion < surface diffusion
The lower the temperature, the larger the contribution of grain boundary diffusion relative to lattice diffusion
The finer the grains, the smaller the contribution of grain boundary diffusion
defects-diffusion-010.explanation: The more disordered the atomic packing along a path, the more easily atoms jump, so the activation energy generally increases in the order surface diffusion < grain boundary diffusion < lattice (volume) diffusion. The choice giving lattice < grain boundary < surface has this order reversed. Paths with lower activation energy lose less of their diffusion coefficient as the temperature falls, so the relative contribution of grain boundary diffusion grows at lower temperatures. Finer grains mean a larger total grain boundary area, so the contribution of grain boundary diffusion actually increases. This is why grain boundary diffusion becomes a problem in low-temperature, fine-grained systems such as solder joints and thin-film interconnects.

defects-diffusion-011.question: When copper and brass (a Cu-Zn alloy) are bonded and heated, inert markers placed at the original interface move toward the brass side (the Kirkendall effect). What does this phenomenon show?
choices: The two kinds of atoms diffuse at different rates, and diffusion proceeds by the vacancy mechanism
Atoms diffuse only by the interstitial mechanism, and the number of lattice sites on each side does not change
Thermal stress generated at the bonded interface during heating is pushing the inert markers toward the brass side
defects-diffusion-011.explanation: Zinc diffuses into copper faster than copper diffuses into brass, so more atoms leave the brass side than enter it. Substitutional diffusion proceeds by exchange with vacancies, so vacancies flow opposite to the net flow of atoms; lattice planes are lost on the brass side and the markers shift toward the brass. This historic experiment showed that diffusion proceeds by the vacancy mechanism. With only the interstitial mechanism, the number of lattice sites would not change and the markers would not move. Excess vacancies that coalesce form Kirkendall voids, which degrade the reliability of solder joints and similar structures.

defects-diffusion-012.question: The Burgers vector of a perfect dislocation in an FCC metal is (a/2)<110>. Which value is closest to its magnitude in aluminum (lattice parameter 0.405 nm)?
choices: About 0.405 nm
About 0.351 nm
About 0.286 nm
defects-diffusion-012.explanation: The magnitude of (a/2)<110> is (a/2) × √(1² + 1² + 0²) = a/√2, so 0.405/1.414 ≈ 0.286 nm. This equals the nearest-neighbor distance in FCC; dislocations take the shortest lattice translation vector along the close-packed direction as their Burgers vector. About 0.405 nm is the lattice parameter itself (a translation along <100>), which is unfavorable because the dislocation energy is proportional to b². About 0.351 nm applies the BCC (a/2)<111>, that is, √3a/2. The elastic energy per unit length of a dislocation is about Gb²/2, so dislocations with smaller b are more stable.

defects-diffusion-013.question: Which statement about the climb of an edge dislocation is correct?
choices: It is motion on the slip plane driven by shear stress, which needs no diffusion and so occurs just as readily at low temperature
It is motion performed only by screw dislocations, which avoid obstacles by switching from one slip plane to another
It is motion out of the slip plane that involves absorbing or emitting vacancies, so it occurs readily at high temperature where diffusion is fast
defects-diffusion-013.explanation: Climb of an edge dislocation is motion in which the edge of the extra half-plane moves up or down, taking the dislocation off its slip plane. Removing atoms from the edge of the half-plane requires absorbing vacancies, and adding atoms requires emitting them, so climb occurs readily at high temperature, where vacancy diffusion is fast. Climb lets dislocations get past obstacles or meet dislocations of opposite sign and annihilate, and it underlies high-temperature creep and polygonization during recovery. Motion on the slip plane is glide, which needs no diffusion. A screw dislocation switching slip planes is cross-slip, which is a different process from climb.

defects-diffusion-014.question: A perfect dislocation in an FCC metal often splits into two Shockley partial dislocations, forming an extended dislocation. Which statement about this is correct?
choices: Splitting into partials increases the sum of the squared Burgers vectors and raises the energy, so it does not actually occur
A stacking fault forms between the two partials; the lower the stacking-fault energy of the metal, the wider their separation and the harder cross-slip becomes
The higher the stacking-fault energy of the metal, the wider the separation of the two partials, and so the easier cross-slip becomes
defects-diffusion-014.explanation: The FCC perfect dislocation (a/2)<110> can split on a {111} plane into two partial dislocations (a/6)<112>. Dislocation energy is proportional to the square of the Burgers vector, and a²/2 falls to a²/6 + a²/6 = a²/3, so splitting is favorable. Between the two partials the stacking sequence is disturbed, forming a stacking fault, and the lower its energy, the farther apart the partials spread. For a screw dislocation to cross-slip, the two partials must first constrict back into one, so in metals with low stacking-fault energy and wide separation (austenitic stainless steel and brass), cross-slip is difficult and work hardening is large. Aluminum has a high stacking-fault energy, and its separation is narrow.

defects-diffusion-015.question: Estimate the energy per unit length of a dislocation as E ≈ Gb²/2. Taking the shear modulus of aluminum as 26 GPa and the magnitude of the Burgers vector as 0.286 nm, which is closest to E?
choices: About 1.1×10⁻⁹ J/m
About 2.1×10⁻⁹ J/m
About 3.7 J/m
defects-diffusion-015.explanation: E ≈ Gb²/2 = 0.5 × 26×10⁹ × (0.286×10⁻⁹)² = 0.5 × 26×10⁹ × 8.18×10⁻²⁰ ≈ 1.1×10⁻⁹ J/m. Per length b of one atom, this is 1.1×10⁻⁹ × 0.286×10⁻⁹ ≈ 3×10⁻¹⁹ J, about 2 eV. A dislocation extends over thousands of atomic lengths, so the gain from configurational entropy is tiny compared with this energy; unlike vacancies, dislocations do not exist in thermal equilibrium and are defects introduced by working or solidification. About 2.1×10⁻⁹ J/m drops the factor of 1/2, and about 3.7 J/m forgets to square b. Because the energy is proportional to b², dislocations take the shortest possible Burgers vector, the shortest lattice vector along a close-packed direction.

defects-diffusion-016.question: In a pure metal, the equilibrium concentration of self-interstitials is far lower than that of vacancies. What is the main reason?
choices: There are far fewer interstitial sites than lattice sites, so there are few places for the atoms to go
Self-interstitials move only with difficulty and cannot reach their equilibrium concentration even at high temperature
Squeezing an atom into an interstice distorts its surroundings strongly, so its formation energy is much larger than a vacancy's
defects-diffusion-016.explanation: The equilibrium concentration of a point defect follows exp(−Q/kT) and falls exponentially as the formation energy Q increases. A self-interstitial, an atom of the host's own size squeezed into an interstice, distorts the surrounding lattice strongly, so in many metals its formation energy is two to several times that of a vacancy, and even near the melting point its concentration is negligible compared with that of vacancies. In FCC there are as many octahedral sites as lattice sites and twice as many tetrahedral sites, so space is not lacking. Self-interstitials also have a small migration energy and are actually more mobile than vacancies. In irradiated metals they are produced in large numbers, paired with vacancies.

defects-diffusion-017.question: When cold-worked copper, brass or austenitic stainless steel is annealed, many annealing twins with straight, parallel boundaries are seen inside the grains. Which statement about them is correct?
choices: Metals with a high stacking fault energy, such as aluminum, form the most annealing twins during recrystallization
They are common in FCC metals with a low stacking fault energy, and a coherent twin boundary has far less energy than an ordinary grain boundary
Twin boundaries have more energy than ordinary high-angle boundaries, so they are the first to disappear during annealing
defects-diffusion-017.explanation: The two regions on either side of a twin boundary are mirror images of each other across the {111} boundary plane. In FCC the stacking sequence of the {111} planes simply reverses at the boundary, so the atomic arrangement is hardly disturbed and the energy of a coherent twin boundary is far lower than that of an ordinary high-angle boundary (about 1/15 to 1/30 of it in copper). How readily twins form is related to the stacking fault energy, and in copper, brass and austenitic stainless steel, which have low values, many annealing twins form during recrystallization and grain growth. In aluminum, with its high stacking fault energy, annealing twins are rarely seen. Because their energy is low, they are not the first boundaries to vanish on annealing either.

defects-diffusion-018.question: One-dimensional non-steady diffusion is described by Fick's second law, ∂C/∂t = D ∂²C/∂x². At a position where the concentration profile C(x) is concave up (∂²C/∂x² > 0), how does the concentration change with time? D is constant and positive.
choices: It rises, because more atoms flow into that position than flow out
It falls, because atoms flow out of that position down the concentration gradient
It depends only on the sign of the gradient: it rises if the gradient is positive and falls if negative
defects-diffusion-018.explanation: Fick's second law combines the first law J = −D ∂C/∂x with conservation of matter, ∂C/∂t = −∂J/∂x. Where ∂²C/∂x² > 0, the flux J decreases with x (∂J/∂x < 0), so more flows into that position than out and the concentration rises. Valleys (concave up) fill in and peaks (concave down) are worn down, so the profile becomes smoother. Whether the concentration rises or falls is set not by the direction of the gradient but by its change (the curvature); even a steep gradient leaves the concentration unchanged if the profile is straight. This is why a linear concentration profile is the steady-state solution.

defects-diffusion-019.question: In a symmetric low-angle tilt boundary made of evenly spaced edge dislocations, the dislocation spacing D is related to a small misorientation θ by D ≈ b/θ. For copper (b = 0.256 nm), which is closest to the dislocation spacing in a boundary with θ = 1.0°?
choices: About 0.0045 nm
About 0.26 nm
About 15 nm
defects-diffusion-019.explanation: θ must be in radians: 1.0° = π/180 ≈ 0.01745 rad. D ≈ 0.256/0.01745 ≈ 14.7 nm, about 15 nm, so one edge dislocation appears roughly every 60 atomic spacings. About 0.26 nm divides by the angle in degrees, 1.0, and about 0.0045 nm multiplies by 180/π instead of dividing when converting to radians. As the misorientation grows, the dislocations crowd together until their cores overlap and they can no longer be distinguished, so beyond roughly 10-15° the boundary is treated as a high-angle boundary. The subgrain boundaries formed during recovery (polygonization) of cold-worked metals are of this type.

defects-diffusion-020.question: When atoms jump randomly in a three-dimensional lattice, the diffusion coefficient is D = Γλ²/6, where Γ is the number of jumps an atom makes per second and λ is the jump distance. For D = 1.0×10⁻¹¹ m²/s and λ = 0.25 nm, which is closest to Γ?
choices: About 2.7×10⁷ s⁻¹
About 9.6×10⁸ s⁻¹
About 1.6×10⁸ s⁻¹
defects-diffusion-020.explanation: Γ = 6D/λ² = 6 × 1.0×10⁻¹¹/(0.25×10⁻⁹)² = 6.0×10⁻¹¹/6.25×10⁻²⁰ ≈ 9.6×10⁸ s⁻¹. About 1.6×10⁸ s⁻¹ forgets the factor 6, and about 2.7×10⁷ s⁻¹ puts the 6 in the denominator, D/(6λ²). Even with about a billion jumps per second, the direction of each jump is random, so the net displacement is only about √(6Dt), roughly 8 µm in one second, far shorter than the total path of about 0.24 m. Atoms vibrate about 10¹³ times per second, so only about one vibration in ten thousand results in a successful jump.

defects-diffusion-021.question: Which statement about a dislocation loop on a slip plane, in which the dislocation line closes on itself, is correct?
choices: The Burgers vector is the same all around the loop: parts normal to it are edge, parts parallel to it are screw, and parts in between are mixed
Because the edge or screw character differs around the loop, the Burgers vector also turns to stay normal to the local line direction
Because the line is closed, the Burgers vector is zero, and the loop moves on its slip plane without straining the surrounding crystal
defects-diffusion-021.explanation: A dislocation line cannot end inside a crystal; it must exit at a surface, close on itself as a loop, or join other dislocations. For a single dislocation, the amount and direction of slip across the boundary between slipped and unslipped regions, that is, the Burgers vector, is the same everywhere. In a loop only the line direction changes from place to place: segments normal to b are edge, segments parallel to b are screw, and those in between are mixed, with both components. Under a shear stress the loop as a whole expands or shrinks. Statements that b varies around the loop or that a closed loop has b = 0 are wrong, and the loop is surrounded by a strain field.

defects-diffusion-022.question: Cold working an annealed metal raises its dislocation density by several orders of magnitude. Which correctly describes the Frank–Read source, one mechanism by which dislocations multiply?
choices: Vacancies cluster into disks, and each disk collapses into one dislocation loop, so dislocations increase regardless of how much the metal is worked
As a dislocation moves, its line spontaneously breaks into two, so the number of dislocations increases in proportion to the distance slipped
A dislocation segment pinned at both ends bows out under shear stress and wraps around, emitting loop after loop while the segment remains
defects-diffusion-022.explanation: A Frank–Read source is a dislocation segment of length L on a slip plane, pinned at both ends by precipitates or dislocation junctions. Under shear stress the segment bows out between its fixed ends, and once it passes a semicircle at a stress of about Gb/L it expands unstably and wraps around the pinning points. Where the wrapped-around parts meet they annihilate, splitting off an outer loop and restoring the original segment, which repeats the process, so one source emits many loops. Loops from collapsed vacancy disks are a separate mechanism seen after quenching and are not the main reason dislocations multiply during working. A dislocation line cannot end inside a crystal, so it cannot break into two as it moves.

defects-diffusion-023.question: In the vacancy mechanism, in which atoms move by exchanging places with vacancies, as in self-diffusion of a pure metal, how is the activation energy Q of the diffusion coefficient expressed? Let E_f be the vacancy formation energy and E_m the migration energy for an atom to jump into a vacancy.
choices: Q ≈ E_m: at equilibrium vacancies are plentiful at any temperature, so only the jump barrier matters
Q ≈ E_f + E_m: both the chance that a neighbor site is vacant and the jump frequency depend on temperature
Q ≈ E_f − E_m: forming a vacancy lowers the jump barrier, so Q is reduced by that amount
defects-diffusion-023.explanation: For an atom to make one jump by the vacancy mechanism, a neighboring lattice site must first be vacant, with a probability proportional to the equilibrium vacancy concentration exp(−E_f/kT). The frequency with which the atom then crosses the barrier into the vacancy is proportional to exp(−E_m/kT). The diffusion coefficient depends on the product of the two, so Q ≈ E_f + E_m. Vacancies are very scarce at equilibrium and their number itself changes strongly with temperature, so taking E_m alone is wrong, and there is no reason to subtract the two. Quenching freezes in high-temperature vacancies, removing the E_f term and speeding diffusion at low temperatures. For interstitial solutes such as carbon, almost all neighboring interstices are empty, so Q is essentially the migration energy alone.

defects-diffusion-024.question: When a fixed amount of solute is deposited as a thin layer on a sample surface and then diffused in (so the total amount of diffusing solute is constant), the surface concentration is C(0, t) = M/√(πDt), where M is the amount of solute per unit area. If the surface concentration after 1 h at a given temperature is C₁, what is it after 4 h at the same temperature?
choices: C₁/2
C₁/4
Still C₁
defects-diffusion-024.explanation: At a fixed temperature D is constant, so the surface concentration is proportional to 1/√t. Four times the time gives √4 = 2, so the surface concentration falls to C₁/2. Equivalently, with the total amount M fixed, the solute spreads to a depth of about √(Dt), so doubling the depth halves the concentration level. C₁/4 wrongly assumes the concentration is inversely proportional to time. A constant value confuses this case with the error-function solution for a fixed surface concentration maintained by continuous supply, as in carburizing. In semiconductor doping, a predeposition at fixed surface concentration is followed by a drive-in with the supply cut off, at constant total amount, to set the depth.

defects-diffusion-025.question: A metal sample is held at high temperature, and the fractional change in sample length ΔL/L and the fractional change in lattice parameter Δa/a measured by XRD are recorded at the same time, both relative to the same reference temperature. If the vacancy concentration (per lattice site) is given by n/N ≈ 3(ΔL/L − Δa/a), which value is closest to it when ΔL/L = 1.85×10⁻² and Δa/a = 1.82×10⁻²?
choices: About 1.0×10⁻⁴
About 3.0×10⁻⁴
About 9.0×10⁻⁴
defects-diffusion-025.explanation: n/N ≈ 3 × (1.85×10⁻² − 1.82×10⁻²) = 3 × 3.0×10⁻⁴ = 9.0×10⁻⁴. When vacancies form, the displaced atoms move to the surface and elsewhere, adding lattice sites, so the volume of the whole sample grows by more than the thermal expansion of the lattice. The XRD lattice parameter reflects only the expansion of the lattice itself, so the difference between the two gives the fraction of lattice sites added by vacancies. The fractional volume change is about three times the fractional length change, hence the factor 3. About 3.0×10⁻⁴ forgets the factor 3, and about 1.0×10⁻⁴ divides by 3. The strength of this method is that it gives the concentration directly, without assuming a vacancy formation energy. If interstitials were the dominant defect, the difference would be negative.
